prompt: Large quantities of plastic waste end up in the world's oceans every year. What do you think are the main reasons for this, and what could be done to address the situation?
essay:
Every year an enormous volume of plastic finds its way from land into the sea, where it breaks into fragments that are effectively impossible to retrieve. The reasons are partly to do with how much plastic we produce and partly to do with what happens to it afterwards.

The first reason is that single-use plastic is extraordinarily cheap to make and almost worthless to collect. A drinks bottle costs a manufacturer very little, so there is no commercial incentive to design it for reuse, and once discarded it is worth so little that recovering it rarely pays for itself. The second reason is that waste infrastructure has not kept pace with consumption. Many fast-growing cities acquired supermarket packaging long before they acquired the collection networks to deal with it, and uncollected waste near a river will eventually reach the ocean whatever anyone intends.

The most effective responses therefore work at the point of production. Requiring manufacturers to fund the collection and disposal of their own packaging changes the arithmetic: a company that must pay to retrieve its bottles has a reason to use fewer of them, or to design them so that retrieving them is cheaper. This should be combined with sustained investment in collection systems in the places where the leakage into rivers is greatest, since better product design cannot help a city that has nowhere to put its rubbish.

Consumer behaviour matters too, though probably less than campaigns suggest. Individual refusal of plastic bags is worth encouraging, but it operates on a fraction of the total volume, and treating the issue as a matter of personal virtue risks distracting from the regulatory changes that would make a measurable difference.
title: Plastic waste reaching the oceans
